Written courses and the synthesis used here

This chapter combines four primary courses from four universities: MIT 6.041 SC, Stanford CS 109, Carnegie Mellon's Introduction to Probability for Computing, and Berkeley STAT 134. Oxford Part B Applied Probability supplies an additional, explicitly bounded reading on conditioning at continuous observations. The source-selection audit records the candidate pool, the material actually read, its fingerprints, and the reasons for selection. It does not claim that every probability course in the world was accessible or examined.

Read the probability axioms and counting chapters first. You need intersections, unions, complements, disjoint partitions, finite and geometric sums, and combinations. No named probability distribution is required for the main arguments: when a success-count formula appears, it is derived by counting disjoint patterns. The chapter develops conditioning on events, multiplication along histories, sampling without replacement, independence, conditional independence, observation protocols, and reliability. Systematic posterior odds, likelihood ratios, and inference with several competing hypotheses belong to the next chapter on Bayes' rule; the ratio identities needed here are proved here rather than assumed.

The instruction and solutions are original English explanations. University exercise structures are identified where adapted; source wording, slides, and figures are not reproduced wholesale. Four translated Iranian examination questions are linked to their original booklet, question number, PDF page, and repository revision. Their answers are derived here and are not presented as an official answer key.

Conditioning defines a new probability measure

What the vertical bar actually means

Let A be the target event and B the information available. With P(B)>0, define

P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B).

The numerator retains the outcomes compatible with both the target and the information. The denominator is the probability mass of every outcome compatible with the information. The result is a proportion within that mass. The bar does not mean division of P(A) by P(B), an implication, a temporal ordering, or a causal intervention. You can condition an earlier event on a later observation. What matters is the specified joint probability model.

In a finite model with outcome weights pω, the conditional weight of an outcome in B is pω/P(B); an outcome outside B receives conditional weight zero. Conditioning preserves ratios among retained weights. It does not make previously unequal outcomes equally likely. If all original outcomes are equally likely, the common weight cancels, yielding |A∩B|/|B|. Counting is a special case of the weighted definition.

Worked weighted example. Four outcomes have probabilities

1/10,2/10,3/10,4/10

. Let A consist of the first and third outcomes and B of the first two. The retained mass is 3/10; the target mass within it is 1/10. Thus P(A∣B)=1/3, whereas simply counting the retained outcomes would incorrectly give 1/2. Reversing the question gives P(B∣A)=1/4. One joint mass can produce two different conditionals because their denominators differ.

Why the ordinary probability laws remain valid

For a fixed positive-probability event B, write Q(E)=P(E∩B)/P(B). Nonnegativity follows from nonnegativity of P; normalization follows from Q(Ω)=P(B)/P(B)=1. If the events Ei are pairwise disjoint, the events Ei∩B are also pairwise disjoint. Countable additivity of P, followed by division by the same positive constant, gives

Q(⋃iEi)=∑iQ(Ei).

Therefore Q is a probability measure on the original event family, with all its mass supported in B. In finite elementary models, we can equivalently use B as the reduced sample space. Every law about probabilities can now be applied to Q consistently. In particular,

P(Ac∣B)=1-P(A∣B),
P(A∪C∣B)=P(A∣B)+P(C∣B)-P(A∩C∣B).

The complement in the first formula is the complement of the target, while the conditioning event stays fixed. In general, P(A∣Bc) is not 1-P(A∣B). These are probabilities in two different conditional spaces. This distinction is central to both calculation and independence questions.

Nested information and null events

Provided P(B∩C)>0, conditioning inside the conditional measure gives

P(A∣B∩C)=P(A∩B∣C)P(B∣C).

To prove this, replace both conditional terms on the right by their original ratios and cancel P(C). Conditioning on B and then on C means retaining their intersection, not averaging their separate conditional answers. If B⊆C up to a probability-zero difference, then B∩C has the same mass as B, so the extra information C is redundant after B.

When P(B)=0, the elementary ratio is undefined. Its numerator is also zero; the quotient is 0/0, not zero or one. The product-definition of independence still makes sense for null events, but the ratio-definition of a conditional does not. A continuous exact observation needs a separately specified conditional distribution or an appropriate limiting construction. The final theory section explains this boundary without smuggling division by zero into a formula.

Source connection. MIT Lecture 2 introduces the reduced universe and explicitly excludes a zero denominator. Stanford's conditional paradigm explains why the probability laws survive. CMU Section 2.3 provides event-level examples. The proof above puts these presentations into one precise measure statement.

Joint tables, feasibility, and reversed conditionals

The four-atom table is a complete model for two events

Write a=P(A), b=P(B), and x=P(A∩B). The four disjoint cells have masses

Cell Mass
A∩B x
A∩Bc a-x
Ac∩B b-x
Ac∩Bc 1-a-b+x

Every mass must be nonnegative. Consequently a joint model exists exactly when a,b∈[0,1] and

max(0,a+b-1)≤x≤min(a,b).

Necessity follows from the four cells. Sufficiency follows by assigning those four nonnegative numbers to a four-outcome probability space; they sum to one. Thus the inequality is an exact existence criterion, not just a loose bound. If a question supplies conditionals inconsistent with it, there is no probability model satisfying all the premises.

For b>0, the feasible range of P(A∣B) is the interval obtained by dividing the two bounds by b. A conditional can exceed the unconditional probability because its denominator has changed; it cannot exceed one. When P(A∣B)=1, the mass of B∖A is zero, which is an almost-sure implication. In a finite model with all singleton weights positive, it is also a literal set inclusion; without that positivity it need not be.

Reconstructing a model from conditional data

Suppose P(B)=b, P(A∣B)=u, and P(A∣Bc)=v, with 0<b<1. The four cells are bu, b(1-u), (1-b)v, and (1-b)(1-v). Therefore

P(A)=bu+(1-b)v.

This is a weighted average, so it lies between u and v. The weights are the population masses of the two strata. The ordinary average (u+v)/2 is valid only when the weights are equal, or when the two rates happen to coincide. If P(A), u, and v are supplied, solve b=(P(A)-v)/(u-v) when u≠v and then check b∈[0,1]. If u=v, compatibility requires P(A)=u and the supplied information does not identify b.

Worked reconstruction. Let b=2/5, u=3/4, and v=1/6. The four cells, in the table's order, are

3/10,1/10,1/10,1/2

. Hence P(A)=2/5 and P(B∣A)=3/4. Equality of these two conditional rates occurs because the marginals are equal; it is not a general symmetry law.

For positive a and b, both reversed conditionals use the same intersection:

P(A∣B)P(B)=P(B∣A)P(A)=x.

They are equal if x=0 or a=b. This covers disjoint positive-probability events as well as equal marginals. Dividing the two conditionals requires x>0; forgetting that condition loses the disjoint case. If P(A∣B)>P(A), then x>ab and, for a>0, P(B∣A)>P(B). The direction of association is symmetric even though the conditional probabilities themselves need not match.

The multiplication rule follows the complete history

Two events, and what happens when a denominator vanishes

Rearranging the conditional definition gives

P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B∣A)

for P(A)>0. Reversing the order gives P(B)P(A∣B) when P(B)>0. No independence is needed. If P(A)=0, the intersection probability is zero directly by monotonicity; do not justify it as zero multiplied by an undefined conditional. In a probability tree, a zero-mass node can simply be terminated because every descendant joint mass is zero.

Many events: proof by telescoping

Define the prefix event Hk=⋂i=1kEi. If all prefixes needed as denominators have positive mass, then

P(Hn)=P(E1)∏k=2nP(Ek∣Hk-1).

Each factor is P(Hk)/P(Hk-1). Adjacent numerator and denominator terms cancel, leaving P(Hn). Equivalently, prove the statement by induction using

P(Hk+1)=P(Hk)P(Ek+1∣Hk)

. Positive probability of the final intersection is a sufficient condition for every prefix to be positive, but is stronger than necessary: the final conditional factor may be zero while all denominators remain positive.

At three stages the rule is

P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B∣A)P(C∣A∩B).

Replacing the last factor by P(C∣B) is an additional modeling assertion. It is valid when the relevant conditional probabilities agree, for example under a suitably stated conditional-independence or Markov property. It does not follow from the multiplication rule. Changing the order of the three events changes the conditional factors but not the final joint mass.

Worked history counterexample. Two independent fair bits are X and Y. Let A={X=1}, B={Y=1}, and C={X=Y}. Then P(A)=1/2, P(B∣A)=1/2, and P(C∣A∩B)=1, giving joint probability 1/4. However P(C∣B)=1/2. The abbreviated product would give 1/8. The observation of A matters after B precisely because it determines whether the bits match.

Trees: multiply down a path, add across incompatible paths

A tree node represents the entire prefix event, not merely the last label. Outgoing conditional probabilities at a positive-mass node sum to one. A leaf's mass is the product of its edge probabilities from the root. Leaves representing different complete outcomes are disjoint, so their masses can be added. The mass of a subtree is the sum of its leaves and is also its prefix mass. These equalities provide internal consistency checks before any conditional ratio is taken.

Worked three-stage calculation. A trial passes stage one with probability 3/5. Given that it passes, it passes stage two with probability 2/3. Given both passes, it passes stage three with probability 1/4. The probability of passing all three is

(3/5)(2/3)(1/4)=1/10

. Its probability of reaching stage three is 2/5; conditional on reaching that stage, its completion probability remains 1/4. The ratio 1/10 divided by 2/5 recovers that conditional. A stage's local success probability and the mass arriving at that stage are different quantities.

Source connection. MIT Lecture 2 provides the three-event tree; Stanford's probability-of-and reading gives the general chain. CMU Theorem 2.10 and Exercise 2.9 motivate the proof. We explicitly separate positive prefixes from positive final mass and do not silently drop historical conditions.

Sequential sampling and exchangeability

Draws without replacement change later denominators

From an urn with r red and b blue objects, draw an ordered sequence without replacement, uniformly among remaining objects at each stage. A specified color pattern with k red positions and m-k blue positions has probability

(r)k(b)m-k(r+b)m,

where

(z)j=z(z-1)…(z-j+1)

and (z)0=1. This notation denotes a falling product, not a power. The numerator tracks how many red and blue objects have been removed; the denominator tracks all removed objects. If the pattern requests too many of a color, its probability is zero. Assume 0≤m≤r+b so a draw of that length is defined.

Every pattern with the same number of red positions has the same probability: the ordering changes where each numerator factor appears but not their product. Thus the sequence is exchangeable, although the draws are usually dependent. Summing over the (mk) disjoint position patterns yields

P(exactly k red)=(rk)(bm-k)(r+bm).

This derivation links an ordered tree to unordered counting. Never count an unordered numerator against an ordered denominator. Replacement with uniform red probability r/(r+b) produces a different model: each fixed pattern then has probability

(r/(r+b))k(b/(r+b))m-k

under independent draws.

Worked example. With four red and three blue objects, the ordered pattern red, blue, red has probability

(4/7)(3/6)(3/5)=6/35

. Exactly two reds in three draws has probability 3(6/35)=18/35. Given that the first two colors differ, the probability that the third is red is 3/5: either retained history has removed exactly one red and one blue. Conditioning on the coarser event is harmless here because the two retained histories give the same remaining counts; it is not harmless in every experiment.

Conditional count information can erase the success-rate parameter

For n independent Bernoulli trials with a common success probability p∈(0,1), every specified binary string with exactly k successes has mass pk(1-p)n-k. Given that the total count is k, all (nk) such strings are equally likely. This statement follows by division by their common total mass, not by assuming every binary string was originally equally likely. Consequently the probability that a specified set of j positions are all successes is

(n-jk-j)(nk)=(k)j(n)j,

with zero numerator when j>k. The parameter p cancels, but the conditioned indicators are dependent. For two distinct positions their joint success probability is k(k-1)/(n(n-1)), which differs from (k/n)2 except at degenerate counts. Equal marginal rates do not restore independence.

Random eligibility: condition on the number selected or combine stages

An object may enter a second stage only if it succeeds in the first. With independent per-object histories and probabilities u for entry and v for success given entry, its overall success probability is uv. For n independent objects, exactly j overall successes has probability

(nj)(uv)j(1-uv)n-j

. This needs independence across object histories; independence between entry and success within an object is not required because v is already conditional. Replacing the random number of eligible objects by its mean generally gives a different distribution. Authentic Question 4 below verifies both the per-object argument and a sum over the random eligible count.

Partitions and total probability, including conditioned weights

Disjoint exhaustive cases

Let Di be a finite or countable partition: pairwise disjoint events whose union has probability one. Ignore zero-mass cells when writing ratios. The target decomposes into disjoint intersections with the partition, so

P(A)=∑i:P(Di)>0P(A∣Di)P(Di).

Countable additivity justifies the countable version. No independence is involved. With an extra positive-mass observation B, the same reasoning inside Q(E)=P(E∣B) gives

For each cell with P(Di∩B)>0, define its conditioned rate qi=P(A∣Di∩B) and its conditioned weight wi=P(Di∣B). Then

P(A∣B)=∑iqiwi.

The sum here runs over the positive-weight cells. A zero-weight cell contributes zero joint mass and does not require a defined conditional rate. This notation keeps the rate and weight visibly separate; it represents exactly the conditional total-probability identity.

Both factors are conditioned consistently. Retaining the original weights P(Di) after observing B is valid only if the weights are unchanged, or if a special cancellation happens. Likewise, replacing P(A∣Di∩B) by P(A∣Di) requires a specific invariance or conditional-independence premise.

Worked conditioned mixture. Half the devices are type one and half type two. Within type one, two checks succeed independently with probability 9/10 each; within type two, independently with probability 1/10 each. Each check has unconditional success probability 1/2, but simultaneous success has probability

(1/2)(81/100)+(1/2)(1/100)=41/100

. Given success on the first check, the probability of success on the second is

(41/100)/(1/2)=41/50

. The first result changes the type weights; it does not change the success rate within a known type.

Conditioning can change the case distribution substantially

If P(N=n)=2-n-1 for n≥0 and each of n independent binary outcomes is zero with probability 1/2, then the joint mass of N=n and all zeros is 2-2n-1. Summing the geometric series gives 2/3. Under the all-zero observation, the conditional mass at n is 3·4-n/4. Its mass at zero is 3/4, so its mass at positive counts is 1/4. The empty collection contributes probability one to the statement that every outcome is zero. Removing it changes the conditioning event. This is the mechanism in authentic doctoral Question 2.

Aggregation and Simpson's reversal

Suppose method A succeeds in 9/10 of easy cases and 2/5 of hard cases. Method B succeeds in 4/5 of easy cases and 3/10 of hard cases. A is better in each stratum. If A receives easy cases with weight 1/10 but B with weight 9/10, their aggregate rates are

9/100+36/100=45/100

and

72/100+3/100=75/100

. The aggregate order reverses because the methods face different case mixtures.

If both methods used the same nonnegative stratum weights summing to one, multiplying each within-stratum inequality by that common weight and adding would preserve the order. Thus the reversal does not contradict arithmetic or the within-stratum comparisons. It signals that aggregate quantities answer a different question. The example is about a probability model, not a causal conclusion about treatment or an observational dataset.

Source connection. MIT's total-probability tree, CMU Section 2.5 and its conditional version, and Berkeley's department-weighting examples motivate this synthesis. The numerical model and its simulation are original.

Independence is a factorization property

Product definition, symmetry, and complements

Events A and B are independent exactly when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). This definition is symmetric and includes zero-probability cases. If P(B)>0, it is equivalent to P(A∣B)=P(A). The equivalence follows by dividing by P(B) in one direction and multiplying in the other. A verbal claim that one event does not influence another must be translated into this specified probability model; absence of a causal connection is not a proof of probabilistic independence.

From independence,

P(A∩Bc)=P(A)-P(A∩B)=P(A)(1-P(B)).

Thus A and Bc are independent. Applying the same argument to Ac gives independence of all four pairs formed by complementing either event. The proof does not divide by either marginal, so it remains valid at boundary probabilities.

Disjoint events satisfy P(A∩B)=0. They are independent if and only if at least one has probability zero. A positive-probability event is independent of itself only if its probability is one: the equation is a=a2. More generally, if A⊆B up to a null difference, independence requires a=ab, so a=0 or b=1. Containment and independence are therefore strongly constrained but not logically incompatible.

Pairwise versus mutual independence

For n events, mutual independence requires product factorization for every nonempty subfamily. Single-event conditions are automatic. The number of nontrivial equalities is 2n-n-1. Pairwise independence checks only the (n2) pair equations. For three events, the three pair equations and the triple equation are all needed; neither set alone implies the other.

Worked XOR model. Two independent fair bits determine A={X=1}, B={Y=1}, and C={X≠Y}. Each has probability 1/2. Every pair intersection has probability 1/4, so the events are pairwise independent. Their triple intersection is empty because two ones cannot differ. Its mass zero differs from (1/2)3. Given A∩B, C is impossible although its marginal is 1/2.

The full-family equation alone does not establish mutual independence. On eight equally weighted outcomes, take A=B={1,2,3,4} and C={1,5,6,7}. All three marginals are 1/2, and the triple intersection is the singleton {1} with mass 1/8=(1/2)3. But P(A∩B)=1/2≠1/4. Thus the triple equation holds while a required pair equation fails. Checking both properties of a counterexample is essential.

Independent coordinate blocks

If all primitive coordinates are mutually independent, events depending on disjoint coordinate blocks are independent. In a finite model, sum the factorized atom probabilities over the two blocks; the double sum factors into the product of the two separate sums. This justifies independent device histories or edge-disjoint network paths built from independent components. Overlapping coordinate blocks do not automatically destroy independence, but the disjoint-block proof is no longer available. One must calculate rather than infer.

For mutually independent events with success probabilities pi, the probability that none occur is ∏i(1-pi), and the probability that at least one occurs is its complement. Exactly one occurs in disjoint patterns, yielding ∑ipi∏j≠i(1-pj). Factoring by ∏i(1-pi) is permitted only if all pi<1; the unfactored sum still works when a success is certain. The familiar homogeneous expression np(1-p)n-1 is a special case, not a substitute for heterogeneous probabilities.

Conditional independence can be created or destroyed

Definition and denominator conditions

With P(C)>0, events A,B are independent given C when

P(A∩B∣C)=P(A∣C)P(B∣C).

When P(B∩C)>0, this is equivalent to P(A∣B∩C)=P(A∣C). To prove it, use the multiplication rule within the conditional measure and divide by P(B∣C). Without that positive denominator, the equality of two ratios is not a valid definition. The factorization definition remains meaningful even when P(B∣C)=0.

Conditional complement closure holds within a fixed conditioning event: if A and B are independent given C, then A and Bc are independent given C. This says nothing by itself about independence given Cc. The complement of a target and the complement of the information play different roles.

Selection can create dependence

Take independent fair bits X,Y and let C={X=Y}. Given C, the two retained outcomes are 00 and 11, each of mass 1/2. Hence

P(X=1∣C)=P(Y=1∣C)=1/2

, but their conditional joint mass is 1/2, not 1/4. The original bits were independent. The selection rule coupled them by retaining only matching outcomes.

Alternatively condition on D={X=1 or Y=1}. The retained outcomes are 01, 10, 11. Each success marginal is 2/3, and their joint mass is 1/3, smaller than 4/9. Conditioning on a common consequence can create negative association as well. This is sometimes called a selection or collider effect; the numerical event calculation is the justification, not the label.

A shared hidden type can create marginal dependence

In the two-device-type example, the checks are independent inside each type but dependent when the type is hidden. More generally let a finite partition have weights wi, and let ui=P(A∣Di), vi=P(B∣Di). Assuming conditional independence in each positive-mass cell,

P(A∩B)=∑iwiuivi,
P(A)P(B)=(∑iwiui)(∑iwivi).

The difference is the weighted covariance of the two rate lists. For two strata with weight w and 1-w, expansion gives

P(A∩B)-P(A)P(B)=w(1-w)(u1-u2)(v1-v2).

Thus the marginal association is positive when both rates change in the same direction and negative when they change in opposite directions. Conditional independence in all strata does not imply marginal independence. In the nondegenerate two-stratum case it implies marginal independence precisely when at least one event's rate is constant across the strata.

Conversely, marginal independence does not imply independence in a stratum, as the matching-bits example shows. One stratum's positive association can cancel another's negative association. Neither marginal factorization nor within-stratum factorization can be transported between probability measures without proof.

Source connection. CMU Definitions 2.11–2.13 and Exercises 2.15–2.21 expose these distinctions. Stanford's independence reading supplies complement closure and the conditional paradigm. Oxford Section 2.3 extends the language to random variables; this chapter confines its formal development to events and finite strata.

The observation protocol belongs in the sample space

A report is an event generated by a reporting procedure

If a message M is produced from a hidden state s, the relevant joint weight is P(s)P(M∣s). Two truthful procedures can assign different message probabilities to the same state. Therefore being told a true statement is not always identical to conditioning on the entire set of states in which the statement is true. It is identical when the specified procedure reports that statement with the same positive probability throughout that set and never outside it.

Two-sensor example. Two independent fair sensors are active or inactive. If a monitor reports whenever at least one is active, the message retains 01, 10, 11 equally; given the report, both are active with probability 1/3. If instead the monitor uniformly chooses one sensor and reports only when that chosen sensor is active, the message probabilities in those three states are 1/2,1/2,1. Their original masses are all 1/4, so the message mass is 1/2 and its joint mass with 11 is 1/4. The answer is 1/2. Truthfulness does not determine the report mechanism.

The two-sided card example

Three cards have face pairs RR, RB, and BB. Select a card uniformly and select its visible face uniformly. The elementary equally likely outcomes are the six card-face pairs. Observing a red face retains three outcomes: two on RR and one on RB. The other face is red in two of those outcomes, so the answer is 2/3. If instead a procedure selects uniformly from the two cards that contain at least one red face and deliberately displays red, the cards have equal retained weight and the answer is 1/2. Naming only the remaining card types erases the different likelihoods of the observation.

A precise door-reveal model

Choose door one among three equally likely prize locations. An informed host always opens an unchosen empty door; when two are available, the host chooses each with probability 1/2. If door three is opened, the joint weights of prize at one, two, and three are 1/6,1/3,0. Divide by their sum 1/2 to obtain conditional probabilities 1/3,2/3,0. Switching succeeds with probability 2/3. If the host instead opens an unchosen door uniformly without knowing the prize and we condition on the opened door being empty, the retained weights differ and switching succeeds with probability 1/2.

Unconditionally, switching under the informed always-reveal protocol succeeds whenever the initial choice was wrong, with probability 2/3, even if the host's tie-breaking is biased. But conditioning on a particular named opened door can depend on that bias. Distinguish the aggregate switching strategy from the posterior after one specific message. These examples are probability calculations under explicit protocols, not magic consequences of the phrase “an empty door was revealed.”

Reliability with shared components

Series, parallel, and overlap

For independent components, a series system works only if all components work, giving ∏ipi. A parallel system works if at least one works, giving 1-∏i(1-pi). Those formulas apply to the component events under the stated independence. They do not authorize treating every path as independent.

Consider a common edge E followed by alternative edges F and G. Assume the three edge states are mutually independent, each with working probability p. The system event is E∩(F∪G). Its reliability is

p(1-(1-p)2)=2p2-p3.

The two path events E∩F and E∩G have joint mass p3, while the product of their marginals is p4. They are dependent for 0<p<1 because they share an edge. Incorrectly applying the independent-parallel formula to these paths gives 2p2-p4, too large by p3(1-p).

Condition on a difficult component to simplify a network

Use a bridge network with vertices source, upper, lower, destination and independent edges: source-upper, upper-destination, source-lower, lower-destination, and upper-lower. All have working probability p. Condition on the bridge edge. If it fails, the two remaining two-edge paths are edge-disjoint, giving 2p2-p4. If it works, upper and lower are connected, so the network works exactly when at least one source-side edge and at least one destination-side edge work. These two pairs are disjoint independent coordinate blocks; the conditional reliability is (2p-p2)2. Weight the two cases:

R(p)=(1-p)(2p2-p4)+p(2p-p2)2.

The conditioning edge is independent of the four remaining edges, so its observation leaves their probabilities unchanged. At p=1/2, the conditional reliabilities are 7/16 and 9/16, giving R=1/2. Always test R(0)=0 and R(1)=1. The truth-table simulation enumerates all 32 edge states; it illustrates and checks this exact reduction.

Animated concept walkthrough

Five fair independent edge states are enumerated; solid gold means working and dashed red means failed.

Choose a concept, then use Play, Next step, Previous step, or the checkpoint slider. Every stop includes its exact state and a complete explanation.

Inspect this exact five-edge configuration: solid gold edges work and dashed red edges fail. Determine whether a working path joins source and destination before adding its atom mass.

Model condition. Edge order is source-upper, upper-destination, source-lower, lower-destination, upper-lower. Each atom has mass 1/32.

Continuous observations and the zero-denominator boundary

Positive-area conditioning still uses the same ratio

Let (X,Y) be uniform on the unit square. Condition on B={X+Y≤1}, a triangle of area 1/2. For 0≤t≤1, the portion of the triangle with X≤t has area

∫0t(1-x)dx=t-t2/2

. Hence

P(X≤t∣X+Y≤1)=2t-t2.

At t=1/2 the value is 3/4, not 1/2. The conditional mass is uniform over the triangle with respect to area, but its projection on the horizontal axis is not uniform because vertical slices have different lengths. Probability geometry requires the correct dimension and the correct underlying density.

An exact real-valued observation is not an ordinary event ratio

For a continuous variable, P(Y=y)=0 at each point. If the variables have a suitably regular joint density and fY(y)>0, a conditional density is defined by

fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX,Y(x,y)/fY(y)

. Integrating it over the target set gives the conditional probability. This is a density ratio, not the ratio of two event probabilities at a point. Conditional versions at individual null points are not uniquely determined by the joint law without a specified convention; the continuous density version is a natural choice under the regularity assumptions.

For a concrete model with density 2 on 0<x<y<1, the marginal density of Y is 2y for 0<y<1. The conditional density of X given Y=y is therefore 1/y on 0<x<y: a uniform distribution on that interval. Its probability of X≤y/2 is 1/2. The elementary quotient

P(X≤y/2,Y=y)/P(Y=y)

would be undefined and supplies no derivation.

One can also condition on the positive-mass strip y≤Y≤y+ε, compute an ordinary ratio, and take a limit under appropriate continuity and domination conditions. For the preceding smooth interior example, the limit agrees with the density answer. Do not claim that every sequence of shrinking events produces the same answer: the limiting geometry can weight the null set differently. Full density theory and regular conditional probability belong to later chapters; this section establishes the boundary needed to avoid incorrect exam manipulations.

Source connection. Oxford Lecture 2, Sections 2.1–2.3, motivates the distinction between a model, its information, and density-based conditioning. Its independence displays contain a printed set-letter typo; the correct event factorization is stated here. This chapter uses only the stated elementary and smooth-density cases and does not claim a proof of general measure-theoretic disintegration.

Fully worked mathematical and conceptual problems

The bank contains 60 worked questions: four authentic translated examinations and 56 original or explicitly adapted problems. Difficulties are author assessments. Several problems ask for a derivation or counterexample rather than a numerical option; their solutions demonstrate the structure needed to recognize a correct examination alternative. Read a statement, inspect its assumptions, and then read the solution as a second explanation. You are not being asked to take an assessment before learning the chapter.

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. At most one independent event

Authentic examination · checked English translation

Phd CS 1404 · Q68 · PDF page 15. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Events B1,…,Bn are independent, and P(Bi)=1/n. What is the probability that at most one occurs? Take n≥2 in the displayed formulas.

1.
(n-1)n-1(2n-1)nn
2.
nn-1(2n-1)(n+1)n
3.
(n/(n-1))n
4.
((n-1)/(n+1))n
Read the complete construction, calculation and checks
  1. No event occurs with probability (1-1/n)n by mutual independence.
  2. Exactly one occurs in n disjoint ways, each of probability (1/n)(1-1/n)n-1. Their total is (1-1/n)n-1.
  3. Add the two cases and factor: (1-1/n)n-1(2-1/n)=(n-1)n-1(2n-1)/nn.
  4. The other options use a different success probability or omit the exactly-one contribution. For n=2 the correct result is 3/4, a quick check against alternatives.

Transfer rule. At most one includes zero; pairwise independence alone would not justify multiplying all complements.

The zero-event and exactly-one cases are disjoint and exhaustive for this target. The exactly-one patterns each require all other events to fail. The formula therefore uses mutual independence of the complete family, including complements, rather than pairwise information. At n=2 direct enumeration gives three of four equally likely event patterns. The stated n≥2 domain also avoids ambiguous endpoint powers in the factored display.

Question 2. A conditional probability with random family size

Authentic examination · checked English translation

Phd CS 1404 · Q69 · PDF page 15. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

The probability that a family has n children is 2-n-1 for n≥0. Independently, each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. Given that the family has no boys, what is the probability it has at least one child?

1.

1/3

2.

1/2

3.

3/4

4.

1/4

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks
  1. Let G mean no boys. Conditional on n children its probability is 2-n, including value one for n=0.
  2. The total probability of G is ∑n≥02-n-12-n=12∑n≥04-n=2/3.
  3. The joint probability of G and at least one child is 2/3-1/2=1/6. Divide by P(G)=2/3 to obtain 1/4, option 4.
  4. The reverse conditional, no boys given at least one child, would be 1/3, option 1. That tempting distractor demonstrates why the conditioning direction must be preserved in translation.

Transfer rule. Name the conditioning event, include the zero-size case where appropriate, and divide the joint event by that event's probability.

The information is the event of no boys, including a family with zero children. Its positive-count joint mass is one sixth and its total mass is two thirds. Reversing the requested direction would instead divide the joint by the positive-count marginal one half and give one third, explaining the tempting first option. The joint event is the same; the denominator changes.

Question 3. Equal heads from unequal sample sizes

Authentic examination · checked English translation

Phd CS 1404 · Q70 · PDF page 16. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Player A tosses a fair coin 25 times and player B tosses a fair coin 20 times, independently. What is the probability that they obtain the same number of heads?

1.
(4520)2-45
2.
(4515)2-45
3.
(4520)2-20
4.
(4515)2-20
Read the complete construction, calculation and checks
  1. Sum over their common head count k: P=2-45∑k=020(25k)(20k).
  2. Replace (20k) by (2020-k) and apply Vandermonde's identity. The sum is (4520).
  3. Alternatively, equal heads means the heads in A's tosses plus the tails in B's tosses total 20. Those 45 independent fair indicators give the same binomial coefficient.
  4. The denominator counts all 45 tosses; 220 is insufficient. The index 15 represents the wrong combined target.

Transfer rule. Convert equality between two counts into one count by complementing one group's successes.

For the complemented-indicator construction, let HA count the first player's heads and let TB=20-HB count the second player's tails. Equality HA=HB is exactly HA+TB=20. Each of the combined 45 indicators is fair and mutually independent. Choosing which 20 are one gives the coefficient in option 1. This independently proves the finite-sum identity rather than merely quoting its name.

Question 4. Heads in a conditional second toss

Authentic examination · checked English translation

MS CE 1405 · Q35 · PDF page 8. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Four fair coins are tossed. Every coin that showed heads is tossed again. If Y is the number of heads in the second toss, what is P(Y=2)?

1.
1/2
2.
3/4
3.
17/128
4.
27/128
Read the complete construction, calculation and checks
  1. Model each coin by two independent fair tosses, with the second revealed only when the first is heads. A coin contributes one to Y exactly on the outcome heads-heads, which has probability 1/4.
  2. The four contribution indicators are independent, so Y is binomial with parameters 4 and 1/4. Exactly two successes have probability (42)(1/4)2(3/4)2=27/128, option 4.
  3. An independent derivation conditions on the number K of first-round heads. Sum (4k)2-4(k2)2-k for k=2,3,4. The contributions are 3/32,3/32,3/128, whose sum is 27/128.
  4. Treating the second round as four unconditional fair tosses ignores that only first-round heads qualify. Fixing the random number of qualifying coins at its expected value also changes the distribution.

Transfer rule. Replace a multistage selection experiment by independent per-object indicators when eligibility and success can be combined into one event.

The latent second toss can be defined even for a coin that is never physically retossed; revealing it only after a first head leaves the observed experiment unchanged. The four independent contribution indicators thus each have success probability one quarter. A failure includes both a first-tail case and a first-head/second-tail case, totaling three quarters. These are the precise events behind the two factors in the binomial count.

Original and course-derived mathematical problems

Question 5. Unequal retained masses

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Four atoms have weights (1,2,3,4). Event A contains atoms one and three; B contains atoms one and two. Find both reversed conditionals and the conditional weight of each atom given B.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Build the conditional measure explicitly. Label the outcomes 1,2,3,4 and write their original probabilities as their weights divided by ten. The information event B={1,2} has probability (1+2)/10=3/10. The conditional measure assigns zero to outcomes 3 and 4 and divides each retained original probability by 3/10:

Q(1)=1/103/10=13,Q(2)=2/103/10=23.

Only outcome 1 also belongs to A, so its conditional weight is the answer. For the reverse direction retain outcomes 1 and 3 instead, with total weight four. The same target atom now has fraction one quarter. As an independent check, multiplying either conditional by its own information probability must recover the same joint mass one tenth. This check would immediately expose using the wrong denominator.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The total weight ten cancels in each ratio. The common intersection has weight one; B has weight three and A has weight four. Thus P(A∣B)=1/3 and P(B∣A)=1/4. Given B, the four atom weights become (1/3,2/3,0,0). Counting two retained atoms as equally likely would give an incorrect answer because conditioning preserves their original weight ratio. The conditional weights sum to one and the two joint identities each recover original probability 1/10.

Question 6. Reconstruct every cell

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Given P(B)=2/5, P(A∣B)=3/4, and P(A∣Bc)=1/6, reconstruct all four joint cells, find P(A), and decide whether A,B are independent.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Construct a normalized joint table before testing independence. The mass in B is 2/5 and its target fraction is 3/4, giving P(A∩B)=3/10. The remaining mass within B is 1/10. The mass outside B is 3/5; its target fraction is 1/6, giving P(A∩Bc)=1/10 and leaving 1/2 outside both.

The two target cells sum to 2/5. Multiplying the marginals gives 4/25, which differs from the intersection 3/10 by 7/50>0. The determinant check gives the same difference: (3/10)(1/2)-(1/10)(1/10)=7/50. Thus the reconstructed table is valid and positively associated, rather than independent. Equal marginal probabilities do not force its internal cells to factor.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Multiply each conditional by its stratum mass. In the order both, A only, B only, neither, the cells are 3/10,1/10,1/10,1/2. They are nonnegative and sum to one, so the data define a valid model. Summing the A row gives P(A)=2/5. Independence would require intersection (2/5)(2/5)=4/25, while the actual value is 3/10. The events are dependent and positively associated. Equal marginals explain the equal reversed conditionals but do not imply independence.

Question 7. An impossible conditional specification

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Can P(A)=1/5, P(B)=3/5, and P(A∣B)=1/2 hold simultaneously? Give a precise reason.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Expose the contradiction as a negative cell. The information mass is 3/5, so its stipulated one-half target fraction demands intersection mass 3/10. But the target's entire marginal is only 1/5=2/10. Completing the four-cell table would require

P(A∩Bc)=P(A)-P(A∩B)=210-310=-110.

A probability measure cannot assign negative mass to an event. No placement of the unspecified outcomes can repair that contradiction, since the intersection is a subset of A. A formal reverse ratio would be (3/10)/(1/5)=3/2, outside the unit interval; this is another symptom of the inconsistent premises, not a permissible answer to the original probability question.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The last two numbers force joint mass P(A∩B)=(3/5)(1/2)=3/10. However an intersection is contained in A and cannot have probability greater than P(A)=1/5. Equivalently the A-only cell would be 1/5-3/10=-1/10, violating nonnegativity. Therefore no probability model satisfies these premises. It is inappropriate to continue computing a reverse conditional from inconsistent data; the feasibility check must precede inference.

Question 8. Sharp range of a conditional

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

If P(A)=7/10 and P(B)=3/5, determine the smallest and largest possible P(A∣B) and construct cells attaining each.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Derive attainability as well as bounds. Write the intersection as x. The target-only, information-only and neither cells are 7/10-x, 3/5-x and x-3/10. Their nonnegativity requires 3/10≤x≤3/5. The information denominator is fixed and positive, so division preserves order and gives 1/2≤P(A∣B)≤1.

At the lower bound all mass lies in the union, with neither cell zero. At the upper bound the information-only cell is zero, so the information event implies the target almost surely. The displayed endpoint tables in the verification below are nonnegative and sum to one. Convexly mixing those endpoint tables preserves both marginals and realizes every intermediate intersection, proving the entire interval is feasible, not merely its endpoints.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The joint mass x lies between 7/10+3/5-1=3/10 and 3/5. Dividing by 3/5 gives the sharp interval [1/2,1]. At the lower endpoint the cells are (3/10,2/5,3/10,0); at the upper endpoint they are (3/5,1/10,0,3/10). Each construction is nonnegative and normalized, so both endpoints are attainable. The upper endpoint says B implies A almost surely; the lower endpoint makes the neither cell empty in probability.

Question 9. Recover an unknown stratum weight

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Events satisfy P(A∣B)=4/5, P(A∣Bc)=1/5, and P(A)=1/2. Find the unknown stratum weight P(B) and the reversed conditional P(B∣A).

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Keep the unknown population weight visible. Let b=P(B). The two disjoint pieces of the target have masses 4b/5 and (1-b)/5. Their sum must equal one half, so

12=4b5+1-b5=15+3b5,b=12.

The common intersection is then 2/5. Reversing the conditional divides that joint mass by the target's marginal one half, giving 4/5. The solution is identifiable because the two supplied stratum rates differ. If they had both equaled one half, the same target marginal would have been compatible with every positive stratum weight; division by their rate difference would then be invalid. The reconstructed positive cells below verify that no impossible rate was introduced while solving for the weight.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Let b be the unknown stratum mass. Total probability gives 1/2=(4/5)b+(1/5)(1-b), hence b=1/2. The joint mass is b(4/5)=2/5, and reversing the conditional gives (2/5)/(1/2)=4/5. The four cells are (2/5,1/10,1/10,2/5), confirming feasibility. The equality of reversed conditionals is explained by equal marginals, not by an automatic symmetry of conditional probability. All denominators in this reconstructed model are positive.

Question 10. Equal reversed conditionals without equal marginals

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

For positive marginal probabilities, characterize when P(A∣B)=P(B∣A). Can they be equal when the marginals differ?

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Avoid division by the common intersection. With positive marginals a,b and nonnegative intersection x, equality of the reverse conditionals is

xb=xa⟺ax=bx⟺x(a-b)=0.

The equivalence multiplies by ab>0, so it remains valid when x=0. There are two branches: a zero joint mass or equal marginals. The unequal-marginal disjoint example below realizes the first branch. If the question additionally required a positive intersection, only the equal-marginal branch would survive. Characterizing the zero set before canceling a factor prevents silently discarding a whole valid family of models.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Write x for the intersection. Equality is x/b=x/a, equivalent after multiplication by positive ab to x(a-b)=0. Therefore either x is zero or the marginals are equal. Positive-probability disjoint events supply unequal-marginal examples: take A mass 1/4 and disjoint B mass 1/2. Both conditionals are zero. Dividing one conditional by the other would wrongly discard this case because that step would divide by zero.

Question 11. Association changes in both directions

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Adapted proof structure: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.8

Assume positive marginals and P(A∣B)>P(A). Prove the corresponding strict inequality for P(B∣A), and identify the quantity that controls both signs.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Use one common signed quantity. Put d=P(A∩B)-P(A)P(B). Subtracting each target marginal from the relevant conditional gives

P(A∣B)-P(A)=dP(B),P(B∣A)-P(B)=dP(A).

Both denominators are positive, so both changes have the sign of d. This proves the requested strict inequality and also the corresponding equality and negative-association statements. Their magnitudes need not agree: for marginals 1/2,1/4 and intersection 1/5, d=3/40, producing increases 3/10 and 3/20 respectively. The same positive association can therefore have different numerical effects in the two conditioning directions.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The given inequality is x/b>a, which is equivalent to x-ab>0 because b is positive. Dividing that same inequality by a gives x/a>b, the desired P(B∣A)>P(B). More precisely the two differences are (x-ab)/b and (x-ab)/a. Their magnitudes can differ but their signs agree. If one marginal is zero its corresponding conditional is undefined, so the positive-marginal premise cannot be dropped.

Question 12. A conditional union uses one universe

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Inside a positive event C, suppose P(A∣C)=2/3, P(B∣C)=1/2, and P(A∩B∣C)=1/3. Find the conditional union, exactly one, and neither.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Resolve four mutually exclusive cases inside the information event. In the measure conditioned on C, put both mass at 1/3. Subtract it from the two target marginals, giving A-only mass 1/3 and B-only mass 1/6. The remaining mass is 1-1/3-1/3-1/6=1/6.

The union consists of the first three cells, exactly one consists only of the middle two, and neither is the fourth. Thus the requested results are 5/6,1/2,1/6. Their interpretation is checked by P(exactly one∣C)+P(both∣C)+P(neither∣C)=1. An unconditional probability of C is unnecessary because all four cells have already been normalized within it.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Apply inclusion-exclusion to the conditional probability measure. The union is 2/3+1/2-1/3=5/6. Exactly one subtracts both copies of the intersection from the sum, giving 2/3+1/2-2/3=1/2. Neither is the complement of the union, giving 1/6. The both, A-only, B-only, neither cells within C are (1/3,1/3,1/6,1/6). Their sum is one; mixing an unconditional intersection into this calculation would break the common universe.

Question 13. Implication in probability versus literal containment

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Construct events with P(A∣B)=1 but B⊈A as sets. Explain why there is no contradiction.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Separate set membership from positive probability. In the proposed three-outcome construction, the exceptional outcome 3 has zero probability. It can still belong to B∖A. The conditional ignores its mass, so the conditional value is one even though the set difference is nonempty.

In general, with P(B)>0,

P(A∣B)=1⟺P(A∩B)=P(B)⟺P(B∖A)=0.

The last equivalence uses the disjoint split of B into its intersection with A and its difference from A. It does not say that the difference contains no outcomes. In a finite space where every singleton has positive probability, a nonempty difference would necessarily have positive mass, so literal containment would then follow. State that support condition rather than silently importing it.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Use three outcomes with weights (1/2,1/2,0). Let A contain only outcome one, and let B contain outcomes one and three. Then P(B)=1/2 and P(A∩B)=1/2, so the conditional is one. Nevertheless outcome three belongs to B but not A. The formula proves only P(B∖A)=0. It establishes almost-sure containment; literal containment follows only with additional support assumptions such as strictly positive weights on every finite outcome.

Question 14. Nested information

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

For weights (1,2,3,4,5), let A={1,4}, B={1,2,4}, and C={1,2,3,4}. Verify the nested-conditioning identity numerically.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

List the retained atoms at each level. The outer information C retains weights 1,2,3,4, totaling ten. The inner event B retains weights 1,2,4, totaling seven. Their intersection is just B, while the target retained inside it has weights 1,4, totaling five.

P(A∩B∣C)=510,P(B∣C)=710,5/107/10=57.

The outer normalizer cancels because numerator and denominator are probabilities under the same outer information. Averaging 5/7 and 5/10 would mix two distinct sample spaces and has no conditional-measure justification. The fifth atom is outside C and contributes to neither term; its positive original weight is irrelevant once that outer observation is fixed.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The total weight is fifteen, but ratios can use unnormalized weights. The intersection B with C is B, of weight seven; its intersection with A has weight five. Thus P(A∣B∩C)=5/7. Inside C, P(A∩B∣C)=5/10 and P(B∣C)=7/10, whose ratio is again 5/7. The cancellation is valid because both C and its intersection with B have positive mass. Averaging P(A∣B) and P(A∣C) would have no justification.

Question 15. A zero last factor is allowed

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Suppose P(A)=2/5, P(B∣A)=3/4, and P(C∣A∩B)=0. Find the triple probability and explain why the chain rule remains defined.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Identify each denominator rather than only the final intersection. The first factor is a marginal 2/5. The denominator for the second factor is this positive mass. Their product gives prefix mass P(A∩B)=3/10, which is the denominator for the final conditional. Both required ratios therefore exist.

P(A∩B∩C)=25340=0.

The conclusion uses multiplication of three defined numbers. A hypothetical fourth conditional given this zero-mass triple would not be defined by the elementary ratio. Its descendant joint probability would still be zero by containment. This distinction explains why “zero times an undefined number” is not an acceptable derivation even when the final joint mass can be established by another argument.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The prefix A has positive mass 2/5, and the second prefix has mass (2/5)(3/4)=3/10. Both denominators used in the chain exist. The last conditional factor is zero, so the triple mass is zero. Positive final mass is not required; it is only a sufficient way of guaranteeing positive prefixes. If a further factor conditioned on the zero-mass triple were written, it would be undefined. A tree should stop that branch rather than multiply an undefined number by zero.

Question 16. Dropping history changes a joint answer

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

For independent fair bits let A={X=1}, B={Y=1}, and C={X=Y}. Compare the correct chain product with the product that conditions C only on B.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Enumerate the entire four-state model. The equally likely states are 00,01,10,11. The triple intersection retains only 11. Given A∩B, equality is therefore certain. Given only B, the retained states are 01,11, only one of which has equal bits.

P(A)P(B∣A)P(C∣A∩B)=1212·1=14,
P(A)P(B∣A)P(C∣B)=121212=18.

The first product matches direct enumeration and the second does not. The missing information specifies the first bit and thus changes the last event's truth. A shorter conditional factor requires a genuine conditional-independence property, not merely the visual appearance of neighboring stages in a tree.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The joint event is the single bit pair 11, so its mass is 1/4. The full factors are 1/2,1/2,1, giving 1/4. Conditioning C only on B leaves two possibilities 01 and 11, so the abbreviated last factor is 1/2 and the product becomes 1/8. The error assumes that observing X adds no information after Y, which is false for the equality event. Pairwise independence of some event pairs does not license this history deletion.

Question 17. Reverse a three-stage factorization

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

P(A)=3/5, P(B∣A)=1/2, P(C∣A∩B)=2/3, P(C)=2/5, and P(B∣C)=3/4. Determine P(A∣B∩C) and state the consistency check.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Compute one joint mass and then divide by the new prefix. In the original order the triple mass is (3/5)(1/2)(2/3)=1/5. In the reverse order the prefix B∩C has mass (2/5)(3/4)=3/10. Thus the requested conditional is (1/5)/(3/10)=2/3.

This ratio is defined and below one, but that alone is not a complete compatibility proof. The explicit six positive cells below sum to one and recover P(A)=3/5, P(A∩B)=3/10, P(C)=2/5 and P(B∩C)=3/10. Their unused two cells can be zero. Constructing a complete joint law proves that no hidden constraint among the supplied marginals prevents the calculation from describing a real model.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The original chain fixes the triple mass at (3/5)(1/2)(2/3)=1/5. The reverse-order prefix has mass P(B∩C)=(2/5)(3/4)=3/10. Dividing gives P(A∣B∩C)=2/3. The triple mass must not exceed either relevant prefix; indeed 1/5≤3/10. The given quantities leave other joint cells unspecified, but they are compatible: choose AB-only and BC-only each 1/10, A-only 3/10, C-only 1/10, and neither 1/5.

Question 18. Conditional paths with a stated Markov assumption

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

An initial bit is one with probability 2/5. At each subsequent step, the next bit differs from the current bit with probability 1/3, independently of earlier history given the current bit. Find the masses of 101 and 111 and their conditional proportions given these are the only retained paths.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Use the history-reduction premise exactly where needed. The initial-one mass is 2/5. Along 101, both transitions change the bit, so the path has weight (2/5)(1/3)2=2/45. Along 111, both preserve it, giving (2/5)(2/3)2=8/45.

The retained event is the disjoint union of these two full paths, with mass 10/45=2/9. Renormalization gives masses 1/5 and 4/5, whose sum is one. Their conditional odds are one to four, equal to the ratio of the original path masses. Conditioning preserves that ratio. Without the stated Markov property, a single-step change rate would not determine the second transition conditional on the first transition's history.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The stated conditional-history property permits use of transition probabilities based on the current bit. Path 101 has mass (2/5)(1/3)(1/3)=2/45. Path 111 has mass (2/5)(2/3)(2/3)=8/45. The retained union is disjoint and has mass 10/45. Dividing gives conditional proportions 1/5 and 4/5. The transition model was an explicit premise; without it, a marginal probability of changing at each step would not determine either path probability.

Question 19. Minimum and maximum of two rolls

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Completed written example: MIT 6.041 SC Lecture 2, PDF page 1

Two independent fair four-sided dice show X and Y. Given min(X,Y)=2, determine the distribution of max(X,Y).

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Start with ordered outcomes. There are sixteen equally likely pairs before observing the minimum. Requiring minimum two excludes every pair containing one and every pair with both entries above two. The surviving five states are 22,23,32,24,42, each of original mass 1/16 and conditional mass 1/5.

The maximum groups these states into disjoint fibers of sizes one, two and two. Their probabilities therefore sum to (1+2+2)/5=1. If unordered pairs were used, the off-diagonal possibilities would need twice the weight of 22; three equal unordered weights would not reproduce the original experiment. The calculation demonstrates that a derived statistic's values need not be equiprobable even when the underlying ordered outcomes are.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The condition retains ordered pairs (2,2),(2,3),(3,2),(2,4),(4,2). They each had probability 1/16, so the conditional universe has five equal atoms. The maximum is two in one atom, three in two atoms, and four in two atoms, giving probabilities 1/5,2/5,2/5. A maximum of one is impossible under the condition. Counting unordered pairs as three equal alternatives would ignore that off-diagonal pairs represent two ordered outcomes.

Question 20. Sampling a specified pattern

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

An urn has four red and three blue objects. Find the probability of red-blue-red without replacement, then the probability of exactly two reds in three draws.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Track inventory after each draw. A first red removes one of four reds from seven objects. A following blue removes one of three blues from the remaining six. A final red then has three available successes among five remaining objects. This produces 36/210=6/35 for the one specified pattern.

For exactly two reds there are three disjoint position patterns. Exchangeability gives each the same factors, though in a different order, so the total is 18/35. The unordered route chooses two of four reds and one of three blues from a three-object subset of seven: 6·3/35=18/35. The agreement checks that ordered and unordered sample representations were normalized consistently. Treating the successive draws as independent would use powers instead of decreasing inventories and fail both derivations.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The specified path has probability (4/7)(3/6)(3/5)=6/35. There are three disjoint color-position patterns with two reds, all with the same numerator factors, so exactly two reds has probability 18/35. Unordered counting confirms (42)(31)/(73)=18/35. The conditional probability of a second red after a first red is 3/6, not 4/7; retaining the original fraction would incorrectly introduce replacement.

This urn walkthrough uses the same initial four red and three blue objects and the exact RBR path.

Question 21. Condition on a coarse color history

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

From the same urn, condition on the first two draws having different colors. Find the probability that the third is red. Explain why ignoring the order is valid here.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Condition on a partition of the retained history. The different-color event is the disjoint union of RB and BR. Each has mass (4/7)(3/6)=2/7, so within their union each weight is one half. Either history leaves exactly three red and two blue objects.

P(R3∣R1B2∪B1R2)=1235+1235=35.

The equal weights are verifiable here, but they are not essential to the final result: any weights summing to one would average two identical rates to 3/5. The reason history compression works is equal remaining composition, not independence of successive draws. A condition retaining RR would require another rate and different weights.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The two retained histories RB and BR each remove one red and one blue. In either case the remaining urn has three red and two blue objects, so the third-red conditional is 3/5. Total conditional probability over the two histories is a weighted average of two identical rates, hence still 3/5 regardless of their weights. One may discard the history order only after establishing this equality of remaining compositions. A different condition, such as at least one red, would retain histories with different compositions.

Question 22. A mixture of remaining urns

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Draw three times without replacement from four red and three blue objects. Given at least one red in the first two draws, what is the probability the third is red?

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Keep both kinds of eligible history. The first-two-draw masses are P(RR)=2/7, P(RB)=2/7, P(BR)=2/7 and P(BB)=1/7. Retaining at least one red gives total mass 6/7, so the three retained histories have conditional weights one third each.

After RR, the remaining red fraction is 2/5. After either mixed history it is 3/5. The required weighted rate is

1325+1335+1335=815.

This gives a second explicit derivation of the subtraction calculation below. The answer lies between the retained-history rates 2/5 and 3/5, providing a convexity check. Selecting a single representative urn would erase the uncertainty about how many red objects were removed.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The conditioning event has mass 1-(3/7)(2/6)=6/7. The joint target can be calculated by subtracting the excluded history from the third-red marginal. By exchangeability the third-red marginal is 4/7. The excluded blue-blue-red path has mass (3/7)(2/6)(4/5)=4/35. Thus the joint mass is 16/35, and the conditional is (16/35)/(6/7)=8/15. Assuming exactly one red has been removed would give 3/5 and overlook the retained RR history.

Question 23. A conditional arrangement erases p

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Eight independent trials have common success probability p∈(0,1). Given exactly three successes, find the probability that positions one and two are both successes.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Count compatible success-position sets. Conditioning on three successes in eight trials retains (83)=56 equally weighted sets of three positions. The equality of those weights follows from their common original mass p3(1-p)5, not from an assumption that all binary strings were initially equiprobable.

Fixing the first two positions leaves one success to choose from positions 3 through 8, giving six favorable sets. Thus 6/56=3/28. The sequential alternative is (3/8)(2/7): after learning that position 1 is a success, two successes remain among seven positions. Its second factor is not 3/8. The changed factor quantifies the dependence created by fixing a total count, even though the original trials were independent.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Every three-success pattern has the same original mass p3(1-p)5, so the conditional patterns are uniform among (83)=56 possibilities. Fixing successes at positions one and two leaves one success to place in six positions. The ratio is 6/56=3/28. Equivalently use (3/8)(2/7). The separate conditional marginals are each 3/8, whose product 9/64 is different; fixing the total introduced dependence. The restriction on p ensures the conditioning count has positive probability.

Question 24. A conditional streak count

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Adapted counting structure: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.24(a); changed trial and success counts

Six independent trials share p∈(0,1). Given exactly three successes, what is the probability they contain a run of three consecutive successes?

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Write the favorable strings before counting starts. Exactly three successes in six positions gives twenty equally likely strings. A run of three must use all three successes. The favorable strings are 111000,011100,001110,000111.

They are distinct and exhaust the possibilities, so the answer is 4/20=1/5. No subtraction for overlapping runs is needed here because two different length-three runs would require at least four successes. If the total number of successes were larger, the same start-counting argument could overcount. This is why the fixed-count premise is part of the proof, not incidental context. The common original pattern weight cancels for every 0<p<1; at endpoint probabilities the stipulated three-success information would have probability zero.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Conditioning makes the (63)=20 three-success strings equally likely. With exactly three successes, a run of three uses all successes, so its start can be one, two, three, or four. These four patterns are distinct and no pattern contains two different length-three runs. The answer is 4/20=1/5. Counting starts by multiplication without checking overlap would fail when more successes were allowed. Here the fixed count makes the events disjoint and makes the answer independent of p.

Question 25. Birthday-type chain with nonuniform labels

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original nonuniform analogue of CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.10

Three independent label draws take values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/2,1/3,1/6. Find the probability that all three labels differ.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Enumerate disjoint permutations, not equally likely label values. The event requires one occurrence of every label. Its six ordered permutations each have product mass (1/2)(1/3)(1/6)=1/36 because the draws are independent. Their disjoint union therefore has probability 6/36=1/6.

The conditional chance of a new label depends on which labels have appeared: after label 1 the unused mass is one half, whereas after label 3 it is five sixths. Thus a uniform birthday-product shortcut would replace genuine history-dependent rates by incorrect common rates. Enumerating complete permutations works because multiplying the same three probabilities in a different order leaves their product unchanged, even though individual labels were never uniform.

Result, interpretation and additional check. All labels differ precisely when the ordered triple is a permutation of 123. There are six disjoint permutations. Each has mass (1/2)(1/3)(1/6)=1/36, so the answer is 1/6. The usual uniform birthday product would be invalid because the labels are not equiprobable. An alternative chain must condition on which labels have already appeared, not only their count: remaining probability mass depends on their identities. Direct disjoint enumeration avoids an unjustified reduction of the state.

Question 26. Random eligibility with unequal stages

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Five objects independently have entry probability 2/3, and conditional success probability 3/4 given entry. Find the probability that exactly two objects succeed overall.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Define the counted event for one object first. An object contributes a success exactly when it enters and subsequently succeeds. Its probability is (2/3)(3/4)=1/2, using the conditional multiplication rule. It fails to contribute with probability one half, combining nonentry and later failure.

For a fixed set of two successful objects, independence across complete object histories gives mass (1/2)2(1/2)3=1/32. There are ten distinct choices of that set, producing 10/32=5/16. This derivation does not assume independence between entry and a later event inside one history; the later rate is already conditional. The expected eligible count 10/3 describes a mean across experiments and cannot replace the experiment's random integer count.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Each complete object history contributes success with probability (2/3)(3/4)=1/2 by the multiplication rule. The independent-history premise makes these five composite indicators mutually independent. A specified two-success pattern therefore has probability (1/2)5, and ten choices of success positions give 10/32=5/16. Replacing the eligible count by 10/3 would not even define the original integer-count experiment. Independence of entry and later success within an object was not required; the latter probability was already conditioned on entry.

Question 27. Total probability needs actual partition weights

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

A source is type one with probability 1/4 and type two otherwise. Its success rates are 4/5 and 2/5, respectively. Find the aggregate rate and the proportion of type-one sources among successes.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Separate population weights, joint success masses and selected weights. Type 1 has original weight one quarter, so its successful mass is (1/4)(4/5)=1/5. Type 2 has original weight three quarters and successful mass (3/4)(2/5)=3/10. Adding the disjoint pieces gives total success mass one half.

Conditioning on success divides each successful type mass by that same half, giving selected weights 2/5 and 3/5. They sum to one. The more reliable type gains relative weight after success, but its within-type success probability and its prior prevalence are different quantities. Averaging the two original rates equally would ignore prevalence and give the wrong aggregate, while using the prior one-quarter weight after selection would ignore the observation.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The two disjoint joint-success masses are (1/4)(4/5)=1/5 and (3/4)(2/5)=3/10. Their sum is 1/2, the aggregate success probability. Within the success event, the type-one mass is (1/5)/(1/2)=2/5. The unweighted average of the two rates would be 3/5, which assumes equal source frequencies. The source proportion increases from 1/4 to 2/5 after success because the type-one success likelihood is larger.

Question 28. A conditioned partition uses new weights

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

D1,D2 are equally likely types. Given D1, observation B has probability 3/4; given D2, it has probability 1/4. Within each type A and B are independent, with A rates 2/3 and 1/3. Find P(A∣B).

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Update the case weights and justify the rates separately. The observed B masses in the two strata are 3/8 and 1/8. Their sum is one half, so conditional stratum weights are 3/4 and 1/4. Within each stratum the stipulated independence says that learning B leaves the A rate unchanged.

Thus P(A∣B)=(3/4)(2/3)+(1/4)(1/3)=7/12. Direct joint addition gives P(A∩B)=1/4+1/24=7/24; dividing by P(B)=1/2 agrees. This independent route checks both the new weights and the rate invariance. Without within-stratum independence, the two marginal rate lists alone would not determine those joint masses.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The B mass is (1/2)(3/4)+(1/2)(1/4)=1/2. Its conditioned type weights are 3/4 and 1/4. Within each type the stated conditional independence keeps the A rates unchanged after B. Therefore the answer is (3/4)(2/3)+(1/4)(1/3)=7/12. Original type weights would yield 1/2 and answer an unconditional question. Without within-type independence, the A rates after B would require additional information.

Question 29. A countably infinite mixture

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

P(N=n)=(1-r)rn for n≥0, with 0<r<1. Conditional on N, N independent checks all pass with per-check probability q∈(0,1). Given that all pass, find the probability that N is positive.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Normalize an infinite sequence of joint weights. Let G denote all checks passing. The joint mass at count n is (1-r)(rq)n, including count zero because an empty collection has no failed checks. The series converges since 0<rq<1 and sums to (1-r)/(1-rq).

After dividing by this sum, the conditional count law is (1-rq)(rq)n. Its zero-count mass is 1-rq, so its positive-count mass is rq. Summing that conditional law directly verifies normalization. Excluding count zero before conditioning would define a different information event, and the question of positive count would then be certain rather than rq. The starting index determines the event being modeled.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The all-pass probability is the convergent sum ∑n≥0(1-r)(rq)n=(1-r)/(1-rq). The zero-count case has joint mass 1-r because an empty collection satisfies all-pass. Subtracting that case and dividing by the total gives 1-(1-rq)=rq. More fully the conditional count law is (1-rq)(rq)n. The distinction between all-pass and at least one pass matters: the latter would exclude the zero-count case from the information itself.

Question 30. Determine whether overlapping cases double-count

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

Events B and C cover the whole space but overlap with positive probability. Is P(A∣B)P(B)+P(A∣C)P(C) necessarily P(A)? Derive the correction.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Expand each weighted conditional into its joint event. The proposed sum is P(A∩B)+P(A∩C). These two events overlap on A∩B∩C. Since B∪C covers the sample space, their union is exactly A.

P(A∩B)+P(A∩C)=P(A)+P(A∩B∩C).

The correction is subtraction of that triple overlap. An explicit example takes B=C=Ω and a target with probability one third: the proposed sum gives two thirds, exactly one extra copy of the target. The simple total-probability formula requires disjoint cases, not merely exhaustive cases. For a particular target the overcount can vanish even if the cases themselves overlap, because their overlap may contain no target mass.

Result, interpretation and additional check. The displayed sum equals P(A∩B)+P(A∩C). Since the union of B and C covers the space, inclusion-exclusion makes this P(A)+P(A∩B∩C). Subtract the overlap mass to obtain the correct result. Thus covering is insufficient for the simple total-probability sum; the cases also need to be disjoint in probability, or their target overlap must vanish. For A equal to the whole space, the overcount is exactly P(B∩C).

Question 31. Simpson reversal in exact fractions

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answer

Original problem

A has success rates 9/10,2/5 in easy and hard cases; B has rates 4/5,3/10. A receives easy cases with weight 1/10 and B with weight 9/10. Calculate the aggregate rates and prove that common weights would prevent this reversal.

Read the complete construction, calculation and checks

Calculate each method under its own case distribution. For method A, the easy contribution is 9/100 and the hard contribution is 36/100, totaling 9/20. For methodBthey are 72/100 and 3/100, totaling 3/4. The reversal is compatible with A's larger within-stratum rates because B receives far more easy cases.

With a common easy weight w, subtracting the two aggregate rates gives w(9/10-4/5)+(1-w)(2/5-3/10)=1/10. This is positive for every 0≤w≤1. Therefore changing only the common mixture cannot reverse these stratum inequalities. No causal superiority conclusion follows from the unadjusted aggregate without specifying how cases were assigned.

Result, interpretation and additional check. Weighted addition gives A rate (1/10)(9/10)+(9/10)(2/5)=9/20. B rate (9/10)(4/5)+(1/10)(3/10)=3/4. A is better within both strata but worse in the aggregate. With a common easy weight w, subtracting the aggregate rates gives w(1/10)+(1-w)(1/10)=1/10>0.
